title: Basic Network Troubleshooting
description: This lesson covers a step-by-step diagnostic process for basic network troubleshooting, moving systematically from local device checks and IP configurations to ping tests, DNS resolution, and layer analysis.
content:
Basic Network Troubleshooting

A practical path from “no connection” to the right next test. Short class report · BSIT fundamentals.

Core Principle: Understand the result first. Fix the problem second. Start close to the device, move outward, and let each command answer one question.

Start Local: Check the Device First

Small physical checks often explain a “network problem” before any command is needed. Start with what you can see.

  • Connection: Is Wi-Fi turned on, or is the Ethernet cable connected?
  • Conditions: Check airplane mode, signal strength, and whether other devices have the same problem.
  • Reset: Restarting the device or reconnecting to the network can clear simple connection issues.

Your IP Address Tells You Where You Are

An IP address identifies the device on the network. These three values describe its local position and its route outward:

  • IPv4 address (Device): Identifies your device on the network.
  • Subnet mask (Local Area): Helps define which devices share the local network.
  • Default gateway (Exit Route): Usually the router sending traffic outside the local network.

Windows Command: ipconfig shows the IPv4 address, subnet mask, and default gateway.

Use Ping to Test One Connection at a Time

Move outward in small steps. The first failed step gives you a useful boundary.

  1. Own device: Ping your own device or local address.
  2. Router: Ping the router or default gateway.
  3. Internet: Ping a known internet address.
  4. Compare: See which step fails before guessing at a fix.

Remember: A successful ping checks basic connectivity, but it does not prove that every app or service is working.

DNS Connects Names to Websites

People use names like [suspicious link removed], but devices connect using IP addresses.

Process: Enter Domain > DNS Resolution > Connect to Site.

When names fail: If an IP address works but a website name does not, DNS may be the problem.

Useful commands:

  • nslookup checks resolution.
  • ipconfig /flushdns clears the resolver cache.

Read the Result Before Changing Settings

The same symptom can point to different layers. Let the test result choose the next question.

  • No local IP: Check the adapter, cable, Wi-Fi, or DHCP connection.
  • Local works, internet fails: Check the router, gateway, or ISP connection.
  • IP works, names fail: Focus on DNS.
  • Only one app fails: The network may be fine. Check the app or its service.

A Simple Troubleshooting Order

Good troubleshooting narrows the problem one layer at a time instead of relying on random fixes.

  1. Connect: Check the physical or wireless connection.
  2. Identify: Check the device’s IP settings.
  3. Test: Test the local device, router, and internet separately.
  4. Resolve: Test DNS and the specific app or website.
  5. Record: Write down what changed and what result you got.
